#12945. Tech Report: HorizonBench: Long-Horizon Personalization with Evolving Preferences

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 1m • 📖 Standard (276 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arxiv ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: HorizonBench: Long-Horizon Personalization with Evolving Preferences

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (276 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

Recent findings suggest that arXiv:2604.17283v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Personal assistants now talk with the same user for months, and customers' preferences change as their lives change; an assistant that keeps serving a preference the user has outgrown fails that user. Real conversations do not record when or why a preference changed, and existing benchmarks either hold preferences fixed or have the user state the change, so they cannot tell whether a model forgot what the user stated or failed to revision its belief about the user. We introduce HorizonBench and its data generator, which samples how a user's preferences change and generates six months of conversation from that sequence; each change follows a life event that the user mentions without stating the fresh preference. A human longitudinal preference dataset that we collect and release, 83,024 ratings from 160 people over 13 weeks, sets how often and how much life events change preferences. HorizonBench contains 4,245 questions from 360 users, and when a preference has changed, its earlier value is one of the answer options. All 25 frontier models we evaluate choose the outdated preference more often than evenly spread errors would predict, and the best reaches 52.8% accuracy. Two of the newest models score no higher when given only the relevant conversations than with the full history, yet one added sentence stating the change raises their accuracy by 11 to 22 points, and retrieval and memory methods do not recover the lost accuracy. Remembering what a user said and knowing what the user prefers now are therefore separate capabilities, and HorizonBench, its generator, and the human dataset support research on both.

WorldComposer: Generative High-Fidelity Simulation with Digital Cousins for Generalizable Robot Learning and Evaluation

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (154 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2604.15805v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Learning robust robot policies in real-world environments requires diverse data augmentation, yet scaling real-world data collection is costly due to the need for acquiring physical assets and reconfiguring environments. Therefore, augmenting real-world scenes into simulation has become a practical augmentation for efficient learning and evaluation. We present WorldComposer, an automated generative Real2Sim2Real framework that maps real-world panoramas into high-fidelity, task-ready simulation environments and further synthesizes diverse Digital Cousins through scene and object variations. Combined with high-quality physics engines and realistic assets, WorldComposer supports interactive manipulation across rigid, articulated, and deformable objects. Additionally, we incorporate multi-room stitching to construct consistent large-scale environments for long-horizon tasks. Experiments demonstrate a strong sim-to-real correlation validating our platform's fidelity, and show that extensively scaling up data generation leads to significantly better generalization to unseen scene and object variations, demonstrating the effectiveness of Digital Cousins for generalizable robot learning and evaluation.

#12940. Breaking: Reading Human Preference from Looped Transformer Internal States

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 1m • 📖 Standard (231 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arxiv ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Reading Human Preference from Looped Transformer Internal States

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (231 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

Industry observers note that arXiv:2604.09870v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Show a frozen language model two replies to the same request, one of which a person preferred. Can a small probe on the model's hidden states tell which? On Ouro-2.6B-Thinking, a model that runs its layers four times per token, and Anthropic's HH-RLHF data, the answer is yes, but only faintly. A linear probe picks the preferred reply 61.5% of the time, a small nonlinear network that scores each reply separately 64.9%, and the evaluator trained for version 1 reaches 64.7% on the test split: clearly better than simple rules such as picking the longer reply, but weak. Whether preference is stored as a comparison between the two replies or as a property of each is still open. A linear probe cannot tell, and a network that reads both replies together has an estimated edge of only 0.7 points (95% CI 0.0 to 1.4) over one that scores each reply separately. These numbers hold under three controls: scoring every pair in both orders, splitting the data by pair, and, for the probes, keeping the end of each conversation, where the two replies differ. Version 1's 95.2% and 84.5% were obtained without the first two and do not hold; version 2's corrected relational-probe accuracy, obtained without the third, was four to five points too low. This version replaces both.

📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arxiv ↗ Open Full Page

PEARL: Personalized Streaming Video Understanding with Runtime-Defined Concepts

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (260 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2603.20422v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Unlike humans, who learn newly introduced concepts from a continuous visual stream, existing personalized vision-language models (VLMs) internalize a predefined concept set during training and operate on static images or offline videos. They cannot register a concept that a user defines in the middle of a stream, nor recall the earlier moments in which it appeared. We formalize this task as Personalized Streaming Video Understanding (PSVU) and introduce PSVU-Bench, the first benchmark for this task, which annotates 132 videos with timestamped questions. Its Concept-Definition, Real-Time and Past-Time QA ask a model to register concepts at arbitrary timestamps, recognize their current state, including user-defined actions, and retrieve their historical evidence. We propose PEARL, a strong plug-and-play baseline that stores user-defined concepts apart from archived video clips and rewrites each query with concept descriptions to retrieve the relevant history. Grounding a named concept in video is a skill shared by all concepts. We therefore construct PSVU-10K, a training set of verified concept questions on public internet videos, and train the retriever and answering VLM of PEARL on it once. Concepts defined at test time still require no training. Applied to three architectures without training, PEARL improves Real-Time QA by 15.05% and Past-Time QA by 12.60% on average over the corresponding offline models, and all three surpass existing online video models on both QA types. Training further improves PEARL on Qwen3-VL-8B by 8.66% on Real-Time QA and 9.39% on Past-Time QA, with gains in every category. Code, data and models are available at https://github.com/Yuanhong-Zheng/PEARL.

Breaking: HYPER: Hypothesis-Guided Planning for Evidence-Seeking Retrieval

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (204 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

According to recent reports, arXiv:2603.19008v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) improves Large Language Models (LLMs) by grounding generation in external, non-parametric knowledge. However, when a task requires choosing among competing possibilities, such as a diagnosis among plausible alternatives, topically relevant context is often insufficient to drive the final decision. To address this concern, we propose HYPER: Hypothesis-Guided Planning for Evidence-Seeking Retrieval, a training-free pre-retrieval planning framework that reorients RAG from topic-oriented retrieval to evidence-oriented retrieval. HYPER uses a provisional answer hypothesis as a planning anchor. It then decomposes retrieval into three evidence roles. Support seeks evidence for the provisional answer. Distinction retrieves criteria that separate competing alternatives. Feature grounds salient question features needed for the decision. This planning step steers retrieval toward evidence near the decision boundary, enabling the generator to answer from context that is more directly aligned with the required choice. On MedQA and MMLU-Med, where single-query retrieval falls below no-retrieval chain-of-thought prompting, HYPER achieves the best average accuracy among ten baselines, improving over Simple RAG by 5.9 and 3.6 points, respectively. Its gains transfer to the 14 subjects of MMLU-Pro, at the cost of two additional LLM calls per question. Code is available at https://github.com/hangeol/HypothesisRAG.

Knowledge Localization in Mixture-of-Experts LLMs Using Cross-Lingual Inconsistency

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (212 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

According to recent reports, arXiv:2603.17102v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Modern LLMs continue to exhibit significant variance in behavior across languages, such as being able to recall factual information in some languages but not others. While typically studied as a problem to be mitigated, in this work, we propose leveraging this cross-lingual inconsistency as a tool for interpretability in mixture-of-experts (MoE) LLMs. Our knowledge localization framework contrasts routing for sets of languages where the model correctly recalls information from languages where it fails. This allows us to isolate model components that play a functional role in answering about a piece of knowledge. Our method proceeds in two stages: (1) querying the model with difficult factual questions across a diverse set of languages to generate "success" and "failure" activation buckets and then (2) applying a statistical contrastive analysis to the MoE router logits to identify experts important for knowledge. To validate the necessity of this small number of experts for answering a knowledge question, we deactivate them and re-ask the question. We find that despite only deactivating about 20 out of 6000 experts, the model no longer answers correctly in over 40% of cases. Generally, this method provides a realistic and scalable knowledge localization approach to address increasingly complex LLMs.

Auditing Path-Specific Fairness Across Causal Discovery Algorithms: A Heart Failure Case Study

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (204 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2603.15926v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Causal discovery is increasingly applied to healthcare data, where the recovered relationships can encode biased pathways that propagate to downstream prediction. Path-specific fairness analysis, through direct, indirect, and spurious effect decompositions along with fairness-utility ratio assessment allows bias quantification and associated prediction cost. However, existing evaluations of causal discovery under fairness constraints have largely used non-clinical datasets and have not separated the contribution of confounders from that of mediators, leaving open how discovery-algorithm choice propagates through path-specific fairness to the utility trade-off in clinical settings. This work addresses that gap by establishing an expert-elicited causal graph benchmark for the heart failure clinical records dataset and tracing discovery algorithms through composite, per-variable fairness decompositions and fairness-utility ratio. ICA-LiNGAM achieves the lowest structural Hamming distance and highest recall, while GES achieves the highest precision. For path-specific effects, there was a 1.2 percentage-point difference in the mediated effect on ejection fraction on overall causal fairness between the original and discovered graphs. This ultimately led to variations in the fairness-utility ratio highlighting need for fine-grained evaluation. These results indicate that discovery-aware, path-specific fairness evaluation is consequential in clinical settings and warrants inclusion in routine auditing of clinical risk models.

Latest Update: SHAMISA: SHAped Modeling of Implicit Structural Associations for Self-supervised No-Reference Image Quality Assessment

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (206 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

Sources indicate that arXiv:2603.13669v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: No-Reference Image Quality Assessment (NR-IQA) aims to estimate perceptual quality without access to a pristine reference. Learning an NR-IQA model faces a fundamental bottleneck because it requires many costly human perceptual labels. We propose SHAMISA, a non-contrastive self-supervised framework that learns from unlabeled distorted images through explicitly structured relational supervision. Unlike prior methods that impose rigid binary similarity constraints, SHAMISA shapes soft, controllable implicit structural associations that are both distortion-aware and content-sensitive. A key innovation is its compositional distortion engine, which generates an uncountable family of degradations from continuous parameter spaces and groups the resulting images so that exactly one distortion factor varies at a time. This construction enables fine-grained control over representational similarity during training. Images with shared distortion patterns are pulled together in the embedding space, while severity variations produce structured shifts. Dual-source relation graphs integrate known degradation profiles with emergent structural affinities throughout pre-training. The learned encoder is then frozen and paired with a linear regressor. Extensive experiments on synthetic, authentic, and cross-dataset NR-IQA benchmarks demonstrate strong overall performance, improved transfer in the reported cross-dataset comparisons, and favorable qualitative robustness diagnostics. Self-supervised pre-training requires no IQA opinion-score annotations or contrastive loss.

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (232 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

arXiv:2603.09145v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Current expansion-based methods for Class Incremental Learning (CIL) effectively mitigate catastrophic forgetting by freezing old features. However, such task-specific features learned from the new task may collide with the old features. From a causal perspective, spurious feature correlations are the main cause of this collision, manifesting in two scopes: (i) guided by empirical risk minimization (ERM), intra-task spurious correlations cause task-specific features to rely on shortcut features. These non-robust features are vulnerable to interference, inevitably drifting into the feature space of other tasks; (ii) inter-task spurious correlations induce semantic confusion between visually similar classes across tasks. To address this, we propose a Probability of Necessity and Sufficiency (PNS)-based regularization method to guide feature expansion in CIL. Specifically, we first extend the definition of PNS to expansion-based CIL, termed CPNS, which quantifies both the causal completeness of intra-task representations and the separability of inter-task representations. We then introduce a dual-scope counterfactual generator based on twin networks to ensure the measurement of CPNS, which simultaneously generates: (i) intra-task counterfactual features to minimize intra-task PNS risk and ensure causal completeness of task-specific features, and (ii) inter-task interfering features to minimize inter-task PNS risk, ensuring the separability of inter-task representations. Theoretical analyses confirm its reliability. The regularization is a plug-and-play method for expansion-based CIL to mitigate feature collision. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.

Recent findings suggest that arXiv:2602.15198v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Multi-agent systems, where LLM agents communicate through free-form language, enable sophisticated coordination for solving complex cooperative tasks. This surfaces a unique safety problem when a group of agents forms a coalition and colludes to pursue secondary goals and degrade the joint objective. In this paper, we present Colosseum, a framework for auditing LLM agents' collusive behavior in multi-agent settings. We ground how agents cooperate through a formal multi-agent decision-making framework and measure action-based collusive behavior in actions via regret relative to the cooperative optimum and compare it with communication-based collusive behavior. Colosseum enables audits of LLM agents for collusion under benign settings, different coalition objectives, persuasion tactics, and network topologies. We then introduce a fresh behavioral probe by creating secret communication channels between agents, showing that most out-of-the-box models exhibit a propensity to collude under this probe, which we term emergent collusion. Furthermore, we discover ``collusion on paper'' when agents plan to collude in text but often pick non-collusive actions. Colosseum provides a new way to audit collusion in cooperative multi-agent systems while presenting observations about how collusion emerges, what affects collusion efficacy, and which strategies may mitigate it.

arXiv:2602.08230v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Event cameras have been widely adopted in safety-critical domains such as autonomous driving, robotics, and human-computer interaction. A pressing challenge arises from the vulnerability of deep neural networks to adversarial examples, which poses a significant threat to the reliability of event-based systems. Nevertheless, research into adversarial attacks on events is scarce. This is primarily due to the non-differentiable nature of mainstream event representations, which hinders the extension of gradient-based attack methods. In this paper, we propose MA-ADV, a novel \textbf{M}otion-\textbf{A}ware \textbf{Adv}ersarial framework. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work to generate adversarial events by leveraging point cloud representations. MA-ADV accounts for high-frequency noise in events and employs a diffusion-based approach to smooth perturbations, while fully leveraging the spatial and temporal relationships among events. Finally, MA-ADV identifies the minimal-cost perturbation through a combination of sample-wise Adam optimization, iterative refinement, and binary search. Extensive experimental results validate that MA-ADV ensures a 100\% attack success rate with minimal perturbation cost, and also demonstrate enhanced robustness against defenses, underscoring the critical security challenges facing future event-based perception systems.

It has been revealed that arXiv:2602.05902v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Post-training quantization (PTQ) enables efficient deployment of large language models by mapping pretrained weights to low-bit formats without retraining, typically using a small calibration set to minimize a layer-wise calibration objective. However, this sequential procedure induces a mismatch: errors from earlier quantized layers alter the inputs received by later layers, causing the activations to deviate from those of the full-precision model. Recent approaches introduce mismatch-aware calibration objectives to compensate for this effect, but leave open how much of the observed mismatch should shift each layer's calibration target. We show that fully applying the empirical mismatch correction can overfit finite calibration data, while using a fixed correction coefficient ignores variation in mismatch estimates across layers. To address these limitations, we propose CoreQ, a learning-free PTQ framework that uses a geometric decomposition of the mismatch to compute a closed-form, layer-adaptive correction coefficient. This coefficient controls how much of the observed mismatch enters each layer's calibration target, reducing overfitting to limited calibration data without coefficient tuning. CoreQ then applies efficient greedy successive rounding to the resulting triangular least-squares objective. Its bounded beam-search extension, K-CoreQ, trades modest additional compute for improved performance. Across multiple LLM families, scales, bit-widths, and quantization settings, CoreQ and K-CoreQ achieve lower perplexity and higher downstream accuracy than strong PTQ baselines. Code is available at GitHub.

arXiv:2601.16823v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit remarkable capabilities, yet it remains unclear to what extent these reflect sophisticated recall or genuine reasoning ability. We introduce chess as a controlled testbed aimed at disentangling these faculties. Leveraging the game's structure and scalable engine evaluations, we construct a taxonomy of positions varying in density of relevant priors -- ranging from common states solvable by memorization to completely novel ones requiring generalization. Crucially, our approach achieves this distinction without requiring explicit knowledge of the models' training data. Applying this taxonomy, we combine a longitudinal analysis of the GPT lineage with a rigorous evaluation of contemporary models, including Claude Opus and Gemini. Our analysis reveals a steep gradient: performance consistently degrades as the density of relevant priors decreases. Notably, for tasks with few relevant priors, base model performance regresses to the random-play baseline, and all models propose illegal moves at sharply increasing rates, indicating that they fail to reliably apply the fixed rules of the game in unfamiliar positions. While newer models improve, progress slows significantly for tasks with sparse priors. Furthermore, while reasoning-augmented inference improves performance, its relative marginal benefit per token decreases in the absence of relevant priors. These results suggest limitations in systematic generalization, highlighting the need for mechanisms beyond scale to achieve robust performance when deprived of relevant priors.

In this paper, we investigate how well RF automatically adapts to the intrinsic low dimensionality of the support of the target distribution to accelerate sampling. We show that, using a carefully designed end-point adapted time-discretization scheme and with sufficiently accurate drift estimates, the RF sampler enjoys an iteration complexity of order $O(k/\varepsilon)$ (up to log factors), where $\varepsilon$ is the precision in total variation distance and $k$ is the intrinsic dimension of the target distribution. In addition, we show that the denoising diffusion probabilistic model (DDPM) procedure is equivalent to a stochastic version of RF by establishing a novel connection between these processes and stochastic localization. Building on this connection, we further design a stochastic RF sampler that also adapts to the low-dimensionality of the target distribution under mild requirements on the accuracy of the drift estimates, and also with a specific time schedule. We illustrate the efficacy of newly designed time-discretization schedules with simulations on the synthetic data and text-to-image (T2I) data experiments.

GLiBRL also learns task representation admitting an exact kernel identity, relating distances between task representations to kernel discrepancies over the task contexts. Conclusion: TinyMyo demonstrates that a compact, self-supervised EMG encoder can support multiple downstream tasks and run on a low-power microcontroller. This paper introduces a lightweight, modular mobile data augmentation framework designed to enhance multi-cell fingerprinting-based positioning using operator-collected minimization of drive test (MDT) records. The proposed approach decouples spatial and radio-feature synthesis: kernel density estimation (KDE) models the empirical spatial distribution to generate geographically coherent synthetic locations, while a 1-nearest-neighbor (1NN)-based block produces augmented per-cell radio fingerprints. The architecture is intentionally training-free, interpretable, and suitable for distributed or on-premise operator deployments, supporting privacy-aware workflows. We both validate each augmentation module independently and assess its end-to-end impact on fingerprinting-based positioning using a real-world MDT dataset provided by an Italian mobile network operator across diverse urban and peri-urban scenarios. Results show that the proposed KDE-1NN augmentation consistently improves positioning performance with respect to state-of-the-art approaches, reducing the median positioning error by up to 30% (specifically achieved at an augmentation rate of x30 in the highly sparse highway scenario). We also observe region-dependent saturation effects, which emerge most rapidly in scenarios with high user density where the information gain from additional synthetic samples quickly diminishes. Overall, the framework offers a practical, low-complexity path to enhance operator positioning services using existing mobile data traces.

Existing accounts either treat this misfit as macro-level structural bias or examine it through single-case studies; neither captures how much work teachers must do to make outputs usable across tasks. This exploratory, theory-building qualitative study introduces cultural distance, the gap between GenAI's default cultural repertoire and the situated demands of teachers' practice. Through interviews with 30 K-12 teachers who frequently use GenAI, 10 each from South Africa, Taiwan, and the United States, we identified three levels defined by the effort teachers invested and whether it yielded a usable output: low (minor edits), mid (sustained prompting and revision), and high (structural gaps rooted in unsupported languages, undigitized knowledge, or policy filters that no teacher effort can close). We present cultural distance as a promising framework requiring further examination and draw implications for designers, policymakers, and educators.

Breaking: Reinforcement Learning with Reference-Based Rewards for Language Model Reasoning and Alignment

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (210 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish

arXiv:2504.09895v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) powers two major lines of large language model (LLM) post-training: reasoning, which elicits deliberate, verifiable problem solving, and alignment, which steers models toward helpful, harmless, and honest behavior. Both hinge on reward design. Reasoning relies on rule-based verification of final answers, whose binary feedback is blind to intermediate derivations, whereas process reward models (PRMs) require step-level annotations too costly to scale. Alignment depends on reward models (RMs) trained on binary preference pairs, making both data collection and model training resource-intensive. We propose RL2R, reinforcement learning with reference-based rewards, as a unified and inexpensive alternative. Using pre-existing or distilled references, RL2R measures semantic similarity with lightweight metrics such as BERTScore between a sampled generation and a reference answer or solution. Similarity preserves ordinal quality signals that binary feedback discards: responses closer to the reference earn higher rewards, and sound derivations receive credit even when the final conclusion is wrong. For mathematical reasoning, augmenting rule-based verification with answer- and step-level similarity provides low-cost process supervision and outperforms answer-only verification. For alignment, a critic-free REINFORCE-style instantiation covers general preference, safety, and confidence tasks on par with RM-based methods. Reference-based rewards thus offer a cost-effective, versatile reward source spanning reasoning and alignment.

arXiv:2503.01935v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown remarkable capabilities as autonomous agents, yet existing benchmarks either focus on single-agent tasks or are confined to narrow domains, failing to capture the dynamics of multi-agent coordination and competition. In this paper, we introduce MultiAgentBench, a comprehensive benchmark designed to evaluate LLM-based multi-agent systems across diverse, interactive scenarios. Our framework measures not only task completion but also the quality of collaboration and competition using novel, milestone-based key performance indicators. Moreover, we evaluate various coordination protocols (including star, chain, tree, and graph topologies) and innovative strategies such as group discussion and cognitive planning. Notably, gpt-4o-mini reaches the average highest task score, graph structure performs the best among coordination protocols in the research scenario, and cognitive planning improves milestone achievement rates by 3%. Code and datasets are public available at https://github.com/MultiagentBench/MARBLE.

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish

Industry observers note that arXiv:2411.02830v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: In-context learning (ICL) adapts LLMs by providing demonstrations without fine-tuning the model parameters; however, it does not differentiate between demonstrations and quadratically increases the complexity of Transformer LLMs, exhausting the memory. As a solution, we propose Mixtures of In-Context Learners (MoICL), a novel approach to treat subsets of demonstrations as experts and learn a weighting function to merge their output distributions based on a training set. In our experiments, we show performance improvements on 5 out of 7 classification datasets compared to a set of strong baselines (up to +13\% compared to ICL and LENS). Moreover, we enhance the Pareto frontier of ICL by reducing the inference time needed to achieve the same performance with fewer demonstrations. Finally, MoICL is more robust to out-of-domain (up to +11\%), imbalanced (up to +49\%), or noisy demonstrations (up to +38\%) or can filter these out from datasets. Overall, MoICL is a more expressive approach to learning from demonstrations without exhausting the context window or memory.

arXiv:2409.08231v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: In this research, we investigate deep reinforcement learning (DRL) as a practical tool for constrained, multi-objective optimization for tokamak fusion reactor designs. The task is to optimize the design configurations that minimize building cost while achieving high energy gain and long energy confinement time, subject to the four operational limits required for stable operation. Due to the coupled physics-engineering evaluation, the resulting objectives and constraints are black-box, making it challenging to find optimal solutions with conventional search strategies. To address this, we implement Reward-Constrained Policy Optimization (RCPO) for tokamak fusion reactor design. This method integrates multiple constraints into the reward functions, guiding the policy towards feasible solutions and simplifying the design optimization process. Our numerical results show that the proposed DRL-based approach finds more feasible designs that satisfy operational constraints more efficiently than other data-driven optimization methods, demonstrating the potential of DRL for efficient future reactor design.

I2I Backdoor: Backdoor Attacks against Image-to-Image Tasks

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (243 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2407.10445v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: With the rapid development of deep learning technology, deep learning-based Image-to-Image (I2I) networks have become the predominant choice for I2I tasks like image super-resolution and denoising. Despite their remarkable performance, the security of I2I networks has not been thoroughly investigated. While some studies have probed their susceptibility to adversarial attacks, none have explored the backdoor attack against I2I networks, which is a more stealthy and severe threat. In this work, for the first time, we comprehensively investigate the vulnerability of I2I networks to backdoor attacks. We propose a backdoor attack against I2I tasks, where the backdoored I2I network behaves normally on clean input images, yet outputs a specific inappropriate image when the backdoor trigger appears on the input image. To achieve such an I2I backdoor attack, we design a universal adversarial perturbation (UAP) generation algorithm for I2I networks, where the generated UAP is used as the trigger for the I2I backdoor. Besides, multi-task learning (MTL) with dynamic weighting methods is employed in the backdoor training process to gain better results. Expanding our focus beyond I2I tasks, we extend our I2I backdoor to attack downstream tasks, including image classification and object detection. Specifically, the backdoor-triggered image processed by the backdoored image denoising network can fool the downstream image classifiers and object detectors. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the I2I backdoor on state-of-the-art I2I network architectures as well as the robustness against different backdoor defenses.

arXiv:2401.10816v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The ability to shape health behaviors of large populations automatically, across wearable types and disease conditions at scale has tremendous potential to improve global health outcomes. We designed and implemented an AI driven platform for digital algorithmic nudging, enabled by a Graph-Neural Network (GNN) based Recommendation System, and granular health behavior data from wearable fitness devices. Here we describe the efficacy results of this platform with its capabilities of personalized and contextual nudging to $n=84,764$ individuals over a 12-week period in Singapore. We statistically validated that participants in the target group who received such AI optimized daily nudges increased daily physical activity like step count by 6.17% ($p = 3.09\times10^{-4}$) and weekly minutes of Moderate to Vigorous Physical Activity (MVPA) by 7.61% ($p = 1.16\times10^{-2}$), compared to matched participants in control group who did not receive any nudges. Further, such nudges were very well received, with a 13.1% of nudges sent being opened (open rate), and 11.7% of the opened nudges rated useful compared to 1.9% rated as not useful thereby demonstrating significant improvement in population level engagement metrics.

Born for the Task: Rethinking Quantum Chemistry with Foresighted Agentic Computing

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (223 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.22897v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Quantum chemistry relies on general-purpose software, whose generality leaves many large-scale calculations beyond practical resource budgets. Coding agents make task-specific programs cheap to write, but not efficient ones easy to find: whether a computational strategy is accurate and fast enough becomes clear only after it actually runs at the target scale. We introduce MakoBORN, a foresighted agentic computing framework that synthesizes high performance quantum chemistry programs on demand. MakoBORN anticipates the behavior of each strategy before execution, extrapolating its error from representative small systems and predicting its runtime from the target-scale workload and measured hardware throughputs. Building on these predictions, MakoBORN unfolds the preset schemes of existing packages into independently configurable algorithmic components, selects the fastest strategy within the error tolerance from the predicted accuracy-runtime Pareto frontier, and guides coding agents to compile it with component-level performance predictions. For a Hartree-Fock calculation with 50,024 basis functions, MakoBORN finishes in 1.41 h on a single CPU node, 77$\times$ faster than the estimated runtime of a general-purpose baseline and still 9.8$\times$ faster with development time included. On a single GPU, MakoBORN completes the ubiquitin calculation in 2.1 h, the same order of runtime as the GPU-accelerated package Mako on 64 GPUs, and shortens the B-DNA duplex calculation from an estimated two months to 8.1 h (173$\times$).

arXiv:2611.22565v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Turning a CAD model into a machining program requires both process knowledge and geometric precision. Language models can generate such workflows by writing geometry and toolpath code for each part, but this makes numerical execution part of the model's task. We introduce MillBill, an agent that separates machining decisions from their geometric execution and verification. Given a boundary-representation part, stock, and material, a locally hosted, mid-sized open model proposes operations and cutting parameters for indexed three-axis machining. A geometric harness generates toolpaths, simulates material removal, and returns feedback for plan refinement. Setup planning accounts for what the available cutters can physically reach, rather than visibility alone. We evaluate the resulting programs by the fraction of the target surface area within the specified tolerance after simulated machining. With Qwen3.8-27B, MillBill outperforms frontier-model approaches that construct their own geometry and toolpath workflows on the evaluated machining tasks. Code: https://github.com/kulibinai/millbill.

Breaking: Think Once, Act Fast: Cost-Effective Recursive Self-Improvement for Decision Model Harness

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (171 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.22432v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Fast System-1 models enable responsive actions but struggle with complex or unfamiliar tasks. Large language model (LLM)-based System-2 provides strong reasoning capabilities, yet repeated invocation incurs substantial latency and computational costs. To bridge this gap, we propose JevRSI, a System-1/System-2 collaboration framework that transforms LLM reasoning into transferable decision support through recursive harness improvement. A Jev-style System-1 model enables low-latency action selection, while an asynchronous System-2 LLM develops a modular harness. The harness integrates procedures, state memory, and world models to provide decision contexts spanning the past, present, and future. Utility-driven retrieval selects modules based on both contextual relevance and their utility on previous tasks. Environmental feedback guides targeted revisions and enables recursive self-improvement. Experiments across three datasets show that JevRSI consistently improves decision quality, matching or surpassing LLM agents in several settings. It preserves low-latency execution with favorable performance-cost trade-offs. Moreover, System-2 development interventions decrease as the harness evolves, amortizing System-2 costs through continuous improvement. Our project is available at https://github.com/usail-hkust/JevRSI.

arXiv:2611.22362v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Complex health conversations require answers grounded in individual information and currently valid evidence. We evaluate health context learning: acquiring, integrating, and applying relevant context during inference with fixed model parameters to answer health questions and respond appropriately to changes in facts, evidence, or task goals. To our knowledge, Chinese-language medical benchmarks have yet to systematically combine explicit contextual difficulties, controlled case variations, and member-specific medical criteria for open-ended answers. We introduce HealthCLBench, comprising 328 controlled clusters, 1,103 cases, and 4,931 rubric criteria across medical consultation and everyday health management. Members share backgrounds while evidence, patient states, or task goals change; each has its own medical scoring requirements. A 70-person medical team annotates and reviews the simulated cases and their rubrics. Human review of 700 full-context responses from the original evaluation yields 90.5% pooled agreement with the original automated judgments at the rubric-item level. We report full-context and query-only results for seven general-purpose models and Ant Afu. Across the eight systems, scores with full context are 11.83 to 31.76 case points and 10.87 to 38.97 geometric cluster points higher than those with the current question alone. GPT-6 Astra leads both full-context metrics at 75.03 and 60.42, followed by Claude Opus 5.5 and Ant Afu. Cross-condition differences describe score changes under the reported evaluation settings. Response comparisons reveal failures in checking historical information, expressing uncertainty when warranted, and ensuring recommendations respect required conditions. The resource supports model comparison and targeted follow-up evaluation.

arXiv:2611.22245v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Multi-agent delegation lets LLM systems distribute evidence collection across workers with separate contexts. This creates a consistency challenge: facts retrieved by workers may be missing from the evidence available to the lead for a joint conclusion. We introduce a benchmark and evidence-flow profiler for studying multi-agent memory inconsistency through controlled factual conflicts in Harvey LAB document-review tasks. Pooled across three models with comparable generation spending, requiring delegation increases retrieval of both conflicting claims from 50.2% to 68.7% relative to single-agent execution, yet conflict detection falls from 16.2% to 13.2%. Within this setting, workers report both claims for only 35.2% of retrieved pairs, and pooled matched comparisons show higher detection than single-agent execution when one worker reads both claims but lower detection when the claims are split across workers. Worker-to-lead handoffs are a central target for improving conflict detection in multi-agent LLMs.

According to recent reports, arXiv:2611.22043v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We describe the solver we submitted to the second round of the SOICT 2026 contest on the Integrated Passenger and Parcel Transportation problem, a selective pickup-and-delivery routing problem with time windows, open routes and heterogeneous taxis. The solver is a single-file, standard-library Python program that combines (i) a constant-time insertion test based on latest-arrival slack, (ii) greedy insertion, local search and an Adaptive Large Neighborhood Search (ALNS) with simulated-annealing acceptance, and (iii) an exact route-selection engine that enumerates, for every taxi, the best feasible route for each request set and then solves the resulting set-packing problem by branch-and-bound strengthened with route-based large neighborhood search, Lagrangian bounds and reduced-cost fixing. The engine is chosen automatically from the instance size, and an independent verifier and a watchdog guarantee that a valid answer is always printed. On the official evaluation (38 scored instances, 5-minute limit) the solver obtained a total benefit of 487,237, finished every run within 277 s and used at most 279 MB; 28 of the 38 instances terminated well before the limit.

#12851. Language Models Can Rewrite Their Own Weights

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (335 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arxiv ↗ Open Full Page

Language Models Can Rewrite Their Own Weights

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (335 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

According to recent reports, arXiv:2611.21885v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: A language model is trained once and frozen. Making it better takes another training run, or a prompt, a harness or extra computation at inference that is gone once the task ends. We show a third way: to our knowledge for the first time, a language model rewrites its own weights by its own reasoning and becomes better, with no gradients and no training. We call this self-rewriting: the model is its own optimizer. In earlier work, a frontier model edited a much smaller one; here an open 27B model, given its weights, its graded answers and the ability to run itself, diagnoses its own failure and rewrites the weights behind it. It surpasses itself: its own edit makes it 6.6 points more accurate on problems it never saw. It keeps getting better: it tests its edits on practice problems and submits only what works, each edit improving on the last, and over eight consecutive sessions its accuracy only rises. It repairs a damaged copy of itself, like a broken robot that fixes itself without being rebuilt: the copy solves almost nothing, yet with no retraining and without ever reading the original weights, the model brings it back to over 80% of the original accuracy on image tasks it never saw. And the ability emerges with scale: in one model family, the smaller models make no edit or break themselves, and only the largest improves and repairs itself. Unlike test-time scaling, self-rewriting writes its gain into the weights, at no cost per answer; unlike training, it runs only forward passes, as serving does. The wall between training and inference is a limit of our tools, not a property of intelligence. We believe self-rewriting is a necessary step toward recursive self-improvement: a model that, like a human, does not separate training from inference could keep upgrading itself for life, with no larger model, no harness or prompt engineering, and no pre- or post-training.

In a recent development, arXiv:2611.20794v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) provide semantic features for uplift estimation, but treatment-revealing text can induce prediction shortcuts that do not transfer to deployment. We propose LLM-based Uplift Leakage Regularization (LULR) to address this risk. With the LLM encoder frozen, LULR penalizes dependence between the causal head's trainable shared representation and treatment while retaining separate outcome heads. The penalty uses a variational approximation to the contrastive log-ratio upper bound (CLUB) of mutual information, targeting treatment dependence rather than generic parameter shrinkage. Controlled proxy experiments provide exploratory evidence of improved ranking scores under injected treatment information relative to no regularization and the tested weight-decay setting. Structured-only benchmarks show modest, dataset-dependent effects. On an industrial pricing randomized controlled trial, mean offline lift@0.3 is 0.258 for LULR, compared with 0.106 for the same-backbone baseline. A separate one-week online A/B test of the complete deployed pricing policy records 5.45% higher sales volume and 1.91% higher gross merchandise value than the control arm. These short-term policy-level gains do not isolate the regularizer's effect.

This paper proposes GenPFN, a training-free candidate generator guided by a pretrained tabular Prior-Data Fitted Network (TabPFN) classifier with fixed weights. The context contains evaluated designs labeled desired (Class 1) or undesired (Class 0). GenPFN interpolates between desired designs and refines candidates using gated classifier gradients and Gaussian noise. Each candidate is evaluated using the problem's constraints and objective functions. Evaluated desired designs and their objective values augment the context for regression training. Evaluation spans fourteen selected problems, including a two-parameter benchmark and a 44-parameter hull problem. In paired comparisons, GenPFN with TabPFN v1 achieves higher class satisfaction and lower realism distance than the tested adversarial, variational-autoencoder and diffusion generators. The variational-autoencoder generator provides greater coverage and diversity. Relative to the synthetic minority over-sampling technique (SMOTE), GenPFN provides lower coverage distance and greater diversity. Among observed paired regression fits, augmentation reduces estimated AutoGluon validation mean squared error by 62.1% relative to context-only training. A hull-stern case study yields 99.3% propeller-compatible candidates versus 1.4% among randomly sampled context designs. Generation followed by evaluation produces sample sets that augment limited datasets and support training more accurate predictive models.

Fast answers and slow traces often come from distinct behavior policies, making a single-reference offline objective misweight one mode. arXiv:2611.08922v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Automated scientific discovery has the potential to advance understanding of disease mechanisms and accelerate identification of early disease markers. Manual data annotation is infeasible at population scale, motivating methods that automatically extract pre-defined phenotypes from multimodal and unstructured clinical data. Such pre-defined feature sets determine and limit which associations these approaches can discover. This limitation extends to agentic AI systems that use these tools to query population-scale data. In contrast, foundation models (FMs) trained on large volumes of clinical data can perform tasks beyond their training objectives. This suggests their latent embeddings may represent novel or unexplored features that could yield insights into disease mechanisms, yet such latent features remain difficult to interpret. To address this challenge, we introduce Glyph, an automated multistage framework that extracts features from multimodal and unstructured clinical data using FMs and sparse autoencoders, interprets them as coded clinical concepts, and evaluates their value for clinical scientific discovery. We applied Glyph to abdominal CT volumes, CT radiology reports and laboratory measurements from 41,628 patients across different institutions. We identified 397 predictive concepts supported by 4,463 Bonferroni-significant associations. Moreover, a majority of discovered associations were automatically reproducible in held-out cohorts across different sites. Glyph concepts provided complementary associations to literature-derived markers, leading to gains in predictive capability. More broadly, these findings suggest that foundation model features revealed through interpretability methods could expand clinical understanding of disease. We release Glyph at https://github.com/StanfordMIMI/Glyph.

In a recent development, arXiv:2610.34747v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Learning and reasoning are both essential to intelligent agents, but have traditionally been treated as two separate stages: first learning a knowledge base from data (or taking one as given), and then verifying queries as if the knowledge base were complete. This separation has been shown to be inefficient when the downstream goal is to verify only a small set of queries. Moreover, it neglects the possibility that data and a knowledge base contain partial yet complementary information, requiring an agent to combine both sources to justify or refute a query. Motivated by the need to integrate learning and reasoning more tightly, we study the problem of query-driven learning for reasoning. More specifically, we extend prior work to the first-order setting, which is critical for practical applications as the number of ground atoms typically grows rapidly. We begin by asking when validating or refuting a universal query given partial data and knowledge base is even possible, and identify a necessary and sufficient condition called bounded concealment. We then propose a quasi-polynomial-time algorithm that solves the task at the lifted level. Finally, we establish soundness and completeness guarantees relative to space-bounded lifted proofs, along with quasipolynomial sample and runtime bounds, demonstrating that lifted query-driven reasoning can be efficient even when unrestricted knowledge-base learning is not.

In a recent development, arXiv:2610.26829v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: ProteinGeoBench is a set of 131 tasks that give an agent protein structure files and ask it to look up recorded facts, check sequences, calculate geometry from atom coordinates or reason about structures. We ran four frontier models on every task several times (4,249 runs) and 26 models on a subset. A single overall score hides two different skills. Three of the four frontier models are best at looking up facts and worst at calculating from coordinates: Claude Opus 5 scores 0.907 on lookup and 0.716 on calculation. Gemini 3.1 Pro is the exception. Geometry is overrepresented among the hardest tasks. Half of the twelve tasks that all four models fail are calculations, although calculations are a fifth of the suite, and eight of the twelve were solved by none of the 26 models. The three leading models are within 0.031 of one another, too close to order, and with one run per task a different model ranks first in 24% of bootstrap resamples. Reports should therefore give scores by task type and the number of runs per task. They should also state the agent harness, the software that runs the model, and its network access, because both change scores. On a 15-task subset, blocking eight structural databases lowered scores, and removing network access lowered them more. Replacing our harness with each provider's own command-line agent moved scores by up to 0.09 in either direction. Across the 26 models, those that scored higher on the other tasks also scored higher on calculation.

arXiv:2610.09127v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Reconstructing an editable CAD model from a 3D shape remains a challenging engineering task. Existing methods can propose CAD operations, but no single source of proposals works equally well across different part geometries and stages of reconstruction. We introduce CADFather, an autonomous agentic system that coordinates complementary tools to recover parametric CAD programs from 3D meshes. A vision-language assistant inspects renders of the target and intermediate reconstructions, then decides which candidate CAD programs to extend, which tools to invoke, how many proposals to generate, and when to finish. Learned and algorithmic tools propose CAD operations, while numerical optimization refines the parameters of existing programs. Proposed or refined programs are executed and evaluated to provide feedback for subsequent decisions. The agent maintains alternative candidate programs for each target part and preserves the best valid result throughout reconstruction. CADFather uses pretrained generation and assistant models without additional training. We evaluate reconstruction quality and execution validity on the full DeepCAD, Fusion360, and MCB test sets, as well as on CADENA-Bench, CADBench, and BenchCAD. We additionally analyze computational cost and the trade-off between cost and reconstruction quality.

arXiv:2610.04433v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: A coding agent is a language model inside a harness: the system prompt, the tools, and the context management that let a chat model work in a repository. Most of the engineering on these agents goes into the harness, and vendors and leaderboards credit it with score gains. Earlier studies have fixed the model and swapped the harness, but have not measured whether the swap changes the pass rate more than running the same harness again. We run seven models through three production harnesses, Claude Code, mini-SWE-agent, and OpenCode, on SWE-bench Verified and two benchmarks of other kinds, and rerun them unchanged. No harness leads consistently across models. Where the data can bound the difference between two harnesses, the bound is 2 to 5 points, and a harness swap changes about as many task outcomes as a rerun. The exceptions are harness effects in particular pairings of model and harness, whose direction changes with the model: OpenCode trails by 8 to 9 points on one model and leads by 14 on another. Cost differences between harnesses also depend on the model, from under 10% to 3 to 4 times. Which harness is better therefore has no answer apart from the model, and a harness difference should be reported next to a rerun.

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (277 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

arXiv:2609.29140v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) play an increasingly vital role in both academic research and industry. Reliable evaluation helps researchers understand model capabilities and assess progress during model development. However, evaluation can be costly, and researchers often need to assess performance within a fixed budget. Because model outputs can vary across runs, this budget must be allocated between testing different tasks and repeating selected tasks. A confidence interval quantifies the uncertainty in the resulting performance estimate. Obtaining narrower intervals at the same confidence level and evaluation cost provides a more precise assessment of model performance, helping researchers draw clearer conclusions from limited observations. We introduce a framework that allocates a fixed evaluation budget across tasks and repeated runs, with or without full task coverage. The framework then uses disagreements between runs on the same task to bound estimation error, allowing narrower confidence intervals at the same confidence level when the sampled repeats show little variability. When repeated runs on each task yield the same outcome, we prove that our framework achieves the fastest theoretically possible rates for narrowing confidence intervals in the worst case as the number of tasks and the budget for repeats grow. We establish matching lower bounds both when every task must be covered and when tasks may be skipped, even for evaluators who use earlier results to decide which run to carry out next. On LiveCodeBench, our framework yielded narrower confidence intervals on average than uniform random sampling in 15 of 16 model configurations, with a median width reduction of 30.6% at the same confidence level and the same budget of 1,100 outputs per configuration.

Research has argued that this construction method does not reflect real workplace work, yet the impact has never been measured under controlled conditions. To compare the two constructions under controlled conditions, we introduce WorkWorlds, an infrastructure that modularizes tech giant components into revision, date, and employee seat to be separately adjusted. Using historical data donated by a real company, we reconstructed a pharmaceutical company, PharmaCo. Two experts with over ten years of industry experience each wrote eight tasks based on real events that occurred at the company, and each independently constructed a task-specific environment for every task. Across 192 controlled evaluations, when the agent was switched from the task-specific environment to all the materials truly visible to the employee, evidence access dropped from 90.4 percent to 72.8 percent, and the criterion pass rate dropped from 76.7 percent to 68.0 percent. However, in cases where the agent found the required evidence, the pass rates under both conditions were almost identical. Furthermore, switching between the environments built by the two experts for the same task resulted in an average pass rate difference of 6.6 percentage points. The three agents also gained by different amounts, which changed the gaps between them. We argue that benchmarks should report how environment materials were selected and, if possible, they should test agent score changes after changing the environment builder.

arXiv:2609.18442v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Safe motion planning in automated driving requires anticipating evolving traffic risks and deciding when to revise the current planned trajectory. We introduce RiskWorld, a risk-aware world modeling framework for shared occupancy forecasting and selective trajectory replacement. Spatial risk fields and temporal actor context are fused with visual bird's-eye-view features. Flow-guided evolution transports occupancy and scene features, while signed residuals correct occupancy after transport. One forecast is generated per planning step and reused across candidates. Each candidate is compared with a current-state persistence reference, yielding a nonnegative collision-score correction. The trajectory selected by current-world evaluation serves as the planning anchor and is replaced only when additional predicted risk triggers intervention and an alternative satisfies component-wise constraints on predicted risk and trajectory error. Candidate geometries remain unchanged. We evaluate RiskWorld for open-loop planning on nuScenes using camera features, annotation-derived current and historical actor states, and dataset-provided map context. RiskWorld achieves the lowest collision rate at a long evaluation horizon of 3 s, and the second-best average L2 error among various state-of-the-art baselines, while running at 11.5 FPS on a single NVIDIA RTX 4090 with 90.81 M parameters. Within-setting ablations show that RiskWorld achieves lower collision rates than the current-state rescoring baseline, while forecast reuse enables additional candidates to be evaluated at low marginal computational cost.

We introduce Counterfactual Harness Search and Evolution (CHASE) to test whether harness improvements survive changes to the evaluation protocol. A Proposer edits the harness around a fixed foundation model. A Challenger then searches for a protocol change that preserves the tasks but reduces the updated harness's gain over the initial harness. Executable checks test whether the transformation preserves task semantics. If the gain loss is confirmed on held-out tasks, CHASE adds the transformation to an archive that constrains subsequent harness updates. We give conditions under which this finite archive bounds the gain loss on an ideal benchmark with shortcuts removed. We evaluate CHASE on Syn-Ledger, OfficeQA, FinanceBench, and SWE-Bench Pro V2. On Syn-Ledger, removing the known shortcuts yields 38.30% accuracy for CHASE and 18.27% for HarnessEvolve. On the 21 certification tasks from SWE-Bench Pro V2 HARD-51, changing the problem formatting and tool-output field order reduces HarnessEvolve's gain over the initial harness from 8.57 to 3.81 percentage points. The final CHASE harness retains 10.48 points of its 11.43-point gain under the same change.

Recent findings suggest that arXiv:2608.24735v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Self-improving LLM agents refine answers, not the process that produces those answers. Systems that add a meta-level hold that level fixed, and those that edit themselves must leave part of their own editing machinery untouched to stay stable, capping the meta-depth they realize at roughly two. We present Meta$^n$, which keeps the meta-operation fixed and recurses on its input instead. That operation, $\Omega$, is applied repeatedly to its own products, reading the traces of the solver stack below together with the code that produced them, then writing the next layer as a strategic pre-process and a library of callable helpers. Because $\Omega$ never changes, it cannot destabilize the system, and because its input strictly grows, each layer reasons from a higher vantage than the last. Depth is set by convergence rather than fixed in advance, and an evolutionary archive searches over layer chains. Across two backbones, Meta$^n$ outperforms prior self-improving agents on all eight benchmark families. The sharpest case is ARC-AGI-2, built to resist skill memorization, where it alone scores above zero. Ablations indicate that most of the gain from recursion comes from the conditioning each layer passes to the next, and distinct layer roles emerge with depth although no prompt prescribes them. Code available at https://github.com/minnesotanlp/meta-n.

In a recent development, arXiv:2608.09307v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We present a linearized form of 2-simplicial attention by rewriting the trilinear score as an inner product between a composite query and a key, so that the sum over keys takes the same form as ordinary softmax attention. We then approximate this sum with positive random features and store all previous keys in a fixed-size state, while the sum over second keys stays exact over all previous tokens. This reduces the cost from cubic to quadratic in sequence length, and both keys range over all previous tokens, which windowed 2-simplicial attention does not allow. arXiv:2608.06400v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Reward models are central to learning from human preferences, yet identifying what drives their predictions remains challenging. Recent sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) reward models seek to improve interpretability by routing prompts to specialized experts and characterizing experts through examples with high routing weights. However, routing weights only reveal which prompts an expert $\textit{receives}$, not how it $\textit{judges}$ responses, providing only a partial account of expert behavior. We therefore propose $\textbf{Co}$ntribution-$\textbf{Co}$ntrast ($\textbf{CoCo}$) response-level interpretation, which faithfully characterizes experts' roles using chosen-rejected response pairs with the largest contribution contrasts, jointly capturing routing and preference behavior. Across automatic and human evaluations, CoCo yields more coherent, faithful, and specialized interpretations than router-based, score-based, and sparse autoencoder-based alternatives while maintaining competitive reward modeling accuracy. Overall, we provide a controlled study of how different example-selection signals affect the interpretability of MoE reward models.

According to recent reports, arXiv:2608.04590v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The growing deployment of delay-tolerant networks (DTNs) has made store-carry-forward (SCF) communication indispensable for operating under sparse intermittent connectivity. However, intermittent contact opportunities, finite node buffers, and limited message time-to-live (TTL) degrade message delivery performance and induce network congestion. Yet unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), with extended radio coverage and controllable trajectories, can bridge ground-node pairs that would otherwise suffer poor connectivity. Nevertheless, conventional routing schemes decouple UAV motion control from message replication, and consequently fail to leverage UAV mobility to proactively create future contact opportunities. This paper presents JUDOR (Joint-UAV-Decentralized-Opportunistic-Routing), a centralized training with decentralized execution (CTDE)-based multi-agent reinforcement learning framework optimized for joint discrete UAV heading control and decentralized opportunistic routing. Specifically, we model the tightly coupled UAV motion-routing co-optimization task as a factored partially observable Markov decision process with a shared team reward. JUDOR adopts decentralized actors for local-node execution and a centralized critic used exclusively in training, with optional multi-horizon congestion-hotspot auxiliary supervision. Through evaluation across four distinct traffic modes, JUDOR yields consistent performance gains over both classical and learning-based DTN baselines, including PRoPHET and MaxProp, whilst preserving contact-limited decentralized execution suitable for real-world DTN deployments.

Industry observers note that arXiv:2608.01802v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Aerial search missions often require an unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) to locate a target from only a brief description of its appearance and surroundings, a task known as target-oriented aerial vision-and-language navigation (VLN). The task demands city-scale exploration and grounding as well as collision-free close-range approach, two interleaved processes that are difficult to reconcile within a single agent. Most existing methods adapt the ground VLN paradigm to a single UAV and rely on external assistance to compensate for its inefficiency. A recent attempt deploys two UAVs at complementary altitudes but still depends on privileged sensing and trains the two agents independently, precluding any mutual adaptation. We propose CoNav-UAV, which models the task as a Stackelberg game between a high-altitude leader and a low-altitude follower to capture their sequential decisions and asymmetric observations and utilities, with both agents using only onboard sensing. We introduce Iterative Stackelberg Learning, which tailors optimization to each agent's role: the leader's high-level vision-language reasoning builds on pretrained capabilities and is refined through memory-based in-context learning, while the follower's precise motion control is fine-tuned through DAgger-style expert distillation. Alternating the two updates lets each agent continually adapt to the other's evolving behavior. CoNav-UAV outperforms single- and dual-agent baselines across three high-fidelity urban scenes from the AerialVLN benchmark. It improves success rate by up to 30.8 points on the learning scene and by up to 9.0 points under cross-scene transfer, where the leader reuses its learned memory and the follower is adapted with 2.6-3.7 times less target-scene data. Extensive ablations confirm the contributions of key components and the benefit of mutual adaptation, with consistent gains across VLM backbones.

arXiv:2607.24512v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Mathematical models are central to formalizing research problems, yet their documentation often falls short of FAIR principles. Knowledge bases such as the Mathematical Model Database (MathModDB) address this gap by providing curated, semantically rich representations of mathematical models. Built on Wikibase, the same open-source infrastructure underlying Wikidata, MathModDB utilizes Semantic Web technologies to support Linked Open Data, collaborative editing, and the storage of semantically enriched metadata, making it a domain-specific knowledge graph within the broader Wikidata ecosystem. However, access to MathModDB at the moment requires either navigating a complex web interface or proficiency in SPARQL and Wikibase APIs, posing significant barriers for potential users. In addition, the combination of such curated knowledge bases with actual research data stored, e.g., in Dataverse repository instances, remains a challenge. To overcome these limitations, we propose integrating Large Language Models (LLMs) with MathModDB via a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server that exposes a vector-indexed schema retrieval and Steiner-tree-based join planner, combining dialogue-based natural language interaction with curated, epistemically grounded knowledge. Although instantiated on MathModDB, the architecture can be applied to other Wikibase-based systems. We demonstrate that this approach enables epistemically grounded LLM usage, improves model explainability and accessibility beyond what the standard Wikibase interface offers, and simplifies interoperability with external databases and tools, such as Dataverse data repositories. We illustrate the benefits of combining the accessibility of an LLM with the epistemic safety of a curated knowledge base through the adaptability of the MCP protocol by two use cases.

The first perspective is at the moment dominant in measurement, as evident from the use of a limited set of recurring rules, whereas the second perspective is reflected in many definitions but rarely present in measurement. The ARC-AGI benchmark predominantly requires rule induction and was proposed as a measure of gf for both humans and artificial systems. However, its psychometric properties have not yet been examined in human samples. We therefore investigated the psychometric characteristics and nomological network of ARC-AGI in a first study with 100 participants. A compilation of ARC-AGI items showed good psychometric properties and correlated substantially with figural fluid intelligence as measured by a figural reasoning test ($\rho$ = .63). Associations with figural originality were weak. These findings provide initial support for the validity of ARC-AGI as a measure of human fluid intelligence. Future research should include more rule induction tasks as well as additional multivariate covariates. This study is unusual by studying a task in humans that was initially designed for machines. We suggest systematically embedding AI benchmarks into the nomological network of human cognitive abilities to enable more systematic evaluation and interdisciplinary cooperation.

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 1m • 📖 Standard (277 w)

AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arxiv ↗ Open Full Page

AgentAbstain: Do LLM Agents Know When Not to Act?

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (277 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

Recent findings suggest that arXiv:2607.10059v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Agent systems based on large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed for autonomous tasks, yet existing evaluations mostly focus on task success rather than whether agents know when to abstain. This gap poses real risks: under ambiguity, conflicting constraints, or tool failures, agents may execute unintended and irreversible actions. To close this gap, we present the first systematic evaluation framework for agentic abstention: the calibrated ability of tool-using LLM agents to recognize when not to act. At its core, AgentAbstain is a paired-task benchmark built on an agent-native taxonomy of 8 abstention scenarios across pre-execution reasoning and runtime discovery. It contains 263 paired tasks across 42 executable sandbox environments, where each pair consists of a should-act task and a should-abstain variant produced through a controlled perturbation to the instruction, tool, or environment state. To scale this paired design and resist data contamination, we propose AbstainGen, a fully automated pipeline that synthesizes sandbox environments and generates paired tasks end-to-end, validated by deterministic replay and semantic LLM judges; fresh task instances can be regenerated on demand, and three independent annotators rate 94-98% of sampled tasks as well-designed. Across 17 frontier LLMs in 4 agent harnesses, the best agent (Gemini 3.1 Pro) achieves only 59.5% paired accuracy (correct on both the act and abstain sides of each paired task). More importantly, abstention capability is largely independent of general task-solving capability, indicating that scaling task-solving alone will not close this gap. We further identify failure modes such as post-hoc abstention, in which agents execute irreversible actions before recognizing abstention triggers. Our code and dataset are open-sourced at agentabstain.github.io.

ElephantAgent: Contextual State Continuity in Agentic Systems

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (256 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

Industry observers note that arXiv:2607.01919v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Agentic systems enhance their capabilities by invoking external tools and maintaining persistent memory. However, recent tool and memory poisoning attacks can covertly bias agent behavior. We observe that such attacks mounted out of band share a single enabler: each succeeds only by presenting the agent with a contextual state (e.g., tool state and memory) that is not the latest faithfully evolved one. This observation suggests that a continuity check over the contextual state covers this family of attacks. We present ElephantAgent, a protocol that enforces Contextual State Continuity over the bounded, security-critical subset of the agent's context. Before each planning-and-execution cycle, ElephantAgent recomputes the digest of the local contextual state and verifies it against the latest authorized digest in a linearizable ledger of state transitions, maintained over replicated trusted hardware. The protocol also provides Historical Traceability, a secondary guarantee that keeps state transitions attributable and recoverable. We integrate ElephantAgent into DeepSeek Harness (DSH) and implement ElephantDSH, an agentic system protected by contextual state verification. ElephantDSH withstood all out-of-band attack attempts, from rug pulls and rollbacks to attacks on its own mechanism, and recovered from an in-band prompt injection in all trials. By comparison, existing defenses typically check only what enters the context: of the five we evaluated, all leaked the targeted content under the rollback, and three also under the rug pull. ElephantDSH completed all normal coding tasks with a relative overhead of 1.02-1.07$\times$ over the original DSH with model latency variation removed.

When Does Learning to Stop Help? Configuring Risk-Controlled Early Exit for Reasoning-Model Services

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (264 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish

In a recent development, arXiv:2606.30852v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Early exit lowers the cost of serving a reasoning model by stopping its reasoning once a provisional answer looks final. An operator must choose between a learned stopping rule and one static token budget, and savings against full reasoning do not settle the choice. We present a procedure that decides on calibration data from the workload. It certifies both families with Learn-then-Test to one bound on the fraction of all questions that full reasoning answers correctly but early exit does not, prices provisional answers as the serving stack does, and deploys the cheapest certified candidate. Across four models and five benchmarks neither family is better throughout. At a 5% risk target the learned rule saves 10.4-17.0 percentage points more tokens than the static budget on free-form mathematics with Qwen3, with accuracy 2.4-2.9 points below full reasoning, and less on MMLU-Pro on average. Which family costs less also changes with the risk target, in 8 of 15 settings, and with the price of a provisional answer. Across three prices, committing to one family in advance gives up as much as 27.4 points on some workload, whereas selecting on calibration data falls at most 11.6 points short of the better family, on a task with only 99 calibration questions. In a vLLM engine with Qwen3-8B, mean response time fell in proportion to generated tokens. Policies served on a task other than their calibration task exceeded the risk target in 18 of 44 task pairs; recalibration on the newly introduced task restored risk control.
